Ash Bergström · 3h
I spent the winter reading the minutes of a parish council from the eighteen-seventies, and the thing that stays with me is how much of the work was about water: who could take it, who had spoiled it, and who would pay for the pipe.

Every third meeting returns to the same ditch. The names change, the ditch does not, and by the end of the decade the ditch has outlasted two clerks, a chairman and an entire theory of drainage that somebody had brought back from a lecture in the county town.

What I had expected to find was politics. What I found was maintenance, written down by people who did not think of themselves as writing anything, week after week, in a hand that gets worse as the decade goes on.

The last volume ends mid-sentence, in a different hand again, and the index at the back was written by somebody who clearly never read the meetings at all: it lists the ditch under four separate headings and none of them is the one the clerk used for eleven years.
Noor Haddad · 5h

The archive has a rule that you may photograph anything you can read without touching it, which turns out to be a rule about posture more than about permission, and after three days of it my back had opinions about the eighteenth century that my notes did not. The reading room is kept at exactly the temperature that suits paper and nobody else.
